title: Developer seeks help finding Drop7 strategy to exceed 1 million points
content:
A developer has posted a project on Hacker News investigating optimal strategies for the puzzle game Drop7. The creator originally wrote a Java program for the game sixteen years ago and recently renewed their investigation to determine if an autonomous strategy can average more than one million points per game. While experienced human players can achieve this score through long-term strategic thinking, the best automated strategies currently developed average between 300,000 and 400,000 points.

The project is described as an experiment in using agents as research collaborators and evidence collectors. The developer has provided a global leaderboard where users can compete and submit human strategies, along with a GitHub repository for the project. The post seeks feedback from individuals with expertise in game theory, stochastic planning, learned value functions, or heavy-tailed evaluation regarding approaches to long-horizon action ranking. The submission has received nine points and has no comments.
summary: A developer is investigating whether an autonomous strategy can average more than one million points in the puzzle game Drop7. Current automated strategies average 300,000 to 400,000 points, while experienced human players can reach one million.
author: Hacker News

title: Vergecast debates if iPhone Duo should have been an iPad
content:
The Vergecast hosts David and Nilay discuss the recent review of the iPhone Duo, which received a score of 7 out of 10. The hosts acknowledge that this rating was not their initial plan and may change over time, citing the difficulty of evaluating a major new concept for the most popular smartphone in history. They debate whether the device deserved its current score and analyze how its perception might evolve.

During the episode, the hosts consider alternative product categorizations for the device. They reference John Gruber of Daring Fireball, who suggested the outer screen is the worst iPhone ever made. The discussion also explores whether the product would be viewed more favorably if it had launched as an iPad rather than an iPhone, or if it were simply named the iPad Duo.
summary: Vergecast hosts David and Nilay discuss whether the iPhone Duo deserved its 7/10 review score. They debate if the device would be better received if it were marketed as an iPad rather than an iPhone.
author: The Verge

title: SpaceX's Starshield throttled, disabling Ukrainian interceptors and causing casualties
content:
Starshield, the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink used by Ukraine, was recently throttled to block terminals traveling above certain speeds. This restriction caused Ukrainian interceptors designed to counter Russian drones to stop functioning at high speeds, facilitating attacks on the country’s energy infrastructure. The disruption reportedly resulted in two deaths and at least 17 injuries. The Ukrainian military stated it received no advance warning of the speed limit.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy characterized the action as a direct message from the US amid rising tensions.
summary: Starshield, the version of SpaceX's Starlink used by the Ukrainian military, was throttled to block terminals traveling above certain speeds. The speed restriction stopped Ukrainian interceptors from working at high speeds, facilitating Russian attacks that resulted in two deaths and at least 17 injuries, and the Ukrainian military said it received no advance warning.
author: The Verge

title: Soundcore Space 2 headphones drop to $106.49 on sale
content:
Soundcore’s newest Space 2 headphones are now available at an all‑time low price of $106.49, a $23 discount from the original $129.99 retail price. The sale is running on Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart, making the upgraded model more accessible for buyers looking for budget‑friendly noise‑cancelling options.

The Space 2 is offered in three colors, including an attractive seafoam green. Customers can choose from the same three color options that were available for the earlier Space One model, ensuring a familiar aesthetic while enjoying the newer hardware.

Key improvements over the Space One include stronger active noise cancellation, especially for low‑frequency sounds such as trains and airplane engines. The headphones also deliver more accurate sound performance thanks to design upgrades, while retaining features that made the original popular, such as support for high‑resolution LDAC audio and the HearID 3.0 personalization tool that lets users adjust the sound profile after listening to sample tracks.

Battery life has been extended to 50 hours with ANC enabled and 70 hours without ANC, up from 40 and 55 hours on the original. The Space 2 also includes a 3.5 mm jack for wired listening when the battery runs low, and it automatically pauses playback when removed, helping users keep their place in songs or podcasts.
summary: Soundcore Space 2 headphones drop to $106.49 on sale.

title: Abandoned Popcorn Time apps disabled to prevent bot army
content:
Researchers at Eye Security discovered that the updater for a Popcorn Time fork named "Time4Popcorn" remains active on numerous Windows, macOS, and Android devices worldwide. The software continues to contact abandoned web domains via unencrypted HTTP and utilizes an outdated, insecure version of Chrome.

The original Popcorn Time application, a torrent-streaming front end, has been abandoned for years despite remaining installed on millions of devices. These dormant installations pose a security risk by potentially forming a bot army, a threat that required the apps to be disabled to prevent exploitation.
summary: Researchers at Eye Security discovered that the updater for the abandoned Popcorn Time fork Time4Popcorn was still active on millions of devices. They disabled the updater to stop the software from phoning home over unencrypted HTTP and joining a bot army.

title: Valve developer Mike Morasky mentions HLX code name at GameSoundCon
content: Gamers still hoping against hope for a true follow-up to Half-Life 2 (after so, so many years ) may remember last year's flurry of speculation that Half-Life 3 was finally nearing completion. Amid all those rumors, though, we never got any official sign from anyone inside Valve that a Half-Life project was currently in development. That changed this week thanks to an apparent slip-up during a panel at GameSoundCon, an industry conference devoted to "the art, technology, and business of game audio." In a panel devoted to Valve's use of open audio engines (captured in this Vimeo clip ), Valve composer and audio artist Mike Morasky let an interesting string of three letters slip while talking about the way the company implements high dynamic range (HDR) audio: Our HDR system is basically that's one of the three pieces that come together to make an HDR that you can easily optimize. And in fact, I think Deadlock has their own version of HDR. HLX has its own version, so on and so forth [emphasis added]. "HLX," of course, has been widely reported as the internal code name for Valve's next Half-Life project. The codename has shown up in Valve engine code since at least 2024, but it has never been referenced in public by a Valve employee until now (though Morasky was responsible for a close call in an interview last year). Read full article Comments
summary: Valve composer Mike Morasky referenced the internal code name HLX while discussing HDR audio during a panel at GameSoundCon. This marks the first time a Valve employee has mentioned the codename associated with the next Half-Life project in a public setting.

title: Knicks sent employees fake offer of championship rings in phishing test: Report
content:
The New York Knicks organization conducted a phishing test by sending employees an email promising free championship rings, according to a report by The New York Times. The message, which was sent in late September, stated, “Congratulations, your Employee Championship Ring is here,” and instructed staff to click a link to select from two ring designs.

The report noted that Madison Square Garden employees who clicked the link were required to attend a mandatory cybersecurity class. This action was taken to address the growing cybersecurity concerns of James Dolan, who is identified as the owner of the Knicks, the New York Rangers, and Madison Square Garden.

Such phishing tests are common in corporate environments to identify employees who may overlook signs of scams. These test emails typically appear to originate from the company but contain telltale indicators of phishing, such as misspelled domains in the sender’s email address.
summary: Knicks sent employees fake offer of championship rings in phishing test: Report.
author: Ars Technica

title: NIH board chair warns RFK Jr.'s vaccine clinic could damage hospital reputation
content:
At a recent meeting of the board that oversees the National Institutes of Health’s Clinical Center Research Hospital, chair Jack Leslie opened with introductions before shifting the discussion to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy. Leslie spent six minutes warning that Kennedy’s anti‑vaccine activities could tarnish the hospital, known as the “house of hope” for patients with rare conditions.  

Leslie criticized a stunt Kennedy staged at the hospital: a surprise ribbon‑cutting ceremony for his vaccine injury clinic. The ceremony featured a panel of individuals claiming to have been injured by vaccines, who sat behind placards reading “vaccine injured” and spoke with Kennedy and other high‑ranking Trump administration officials.  

Leslie said some might prefer he remain silent, but he believes silence would be a failing for the advisory board. He added that he has no concerns about studying potential vaccine injuries, noting that serious reactions are rare but real and that people who believe they have been injured should be taken seriously.
summary: Jack Leslie, chair of the NIH Clinical Center board, stated that Robert F. Kennedy's surprise appearance at a vaccine injury clinic opening could tarnish the hospital. Leslie warned that the event, which featured individuals claiming vaccine injuries, risks damaging the institution's reputation despite his support for studying rare reactions.

title: Intel gets FCC waiver to use foreign-made robots in US fabs
content:
Intel secured a temporary exemption from a U.S. government ban that had raised concerns about the use of foreign‑made robots in its chip‑making facilities. The company requested a waiver to ensure it could continue deploying certain robotic vehicles in its U.S. semiconductor fabs. The Federal Communications Commission, which had issued the ban on specific foreign‑made robots, granted Intel’s request in an order published on October 22. The exemption allows Intel to use the robots for a period of one year.

The robots in question are automated guided vehicles that operate on tracks or predefined paths and typically require operator oversight. According to Intel’s website, these vehicles move materials and items around warehouses and factory floors. The FCC’s decision clarifies that Intel may maintain these robotic systems in its U.S. manufacturing plants despite the broader regulatory restrictions.
summary: Intel requested and received a one-year waiver from the FCC to continue using foreign-made automated guided vehicles in its US semiconductor manufacturing facilities. The agency granted the waiver on October 22 after Intel sought clarification due to uncertainty surrounding a ban on certain foreign-made robots.

title: Crows Evaluate Visual Information Twice as Fast as Mammals
content:
Neurobiologist Andreas Nieder of the University of Tübingen highlighted a significant gap in understanding how avian brains process visual information, noting that birds lack the neocortex found in mammals. While research on monkeys using random-dot-motion tasks has established that primate neocortex neurons accumulate visual evidence over time until a decision threshold is crossed, it remained unclear how differently organized avian brains encode similar decisions. Nieder described this mechanism as the central question in the field.

The provided text indicates that crows can evaluate visual information twice as fast as mammals, a finding that addresses how these birds make decisions despite their distinct brain structure. This discovery offers insight into the neural processes underlying decision-making in species without a neocortex, contrasting with the well-documented evidence-gathering mechanisms observed in primate studies.
summary: In a random‑dot‑motion task, primates gather visual evidence until a threshold is reached, prompting a decision. Researchers at the University of Tübingen found that crows evaluate visual information twice as fast as mammals, raising questions about how avian brains encode decisions without a neocortex.

content: The United States has declared helium a critical material. The decision follows a global supply squeeze caused by war in the Middle East and export curbs imposed by Russia and China. Helium is essential for chipmaking, and Europe is scrambling to secure its share of the limited supply.

content:
France is preparing for another weekend of protests after violence erupted during last week’s mobilisations. Paris has extended a partial curfew in parts of the city until Monday, while protests are banned altogether in Marseille and Lyon.  

70,000 security personnel will be deployed on Saturday, and only union demonstrations will be authorised.

content: It's been a week that’s seen mass protests hijacked by violent rioters across France. The looting of shops, trashing of public buildings, the burning of Lyon’s Tourist Information and the iconic Limoges City Hall. After the riots, came the curfews, and the contemplation, who did what and why weren’t they stopped. Seditious groups, ultra left anarchists and opportunist criminals said President Macron, with a qualified mea culpa: failures in anticipation and authorities dropped the ball in intelligence gathering. content:
Storm Austen, the first named storm of the year, struck south‑west England, prompting school closures and widespread power outages. A gust of 76 mph was recorded at St Mary’s airport on the Isles of Scilly on Friday morning, and just before 11 a.m. National Grid reported that more than 16,000 homes in the region were without electricity.

Dozens of schools in Cornwall were also affected. Meanwhile, Storm Boelo is moving toward Scotland, Northern Ireland and the north of England.

title: Study finds stupendously large black holes are not a major component of dark matter
content:
A new study indicates that black holes with masses exceeding that of entire galaxies are not a primary component of dark matter. Dark matter is a hypothetical substance believed to constitute approximately five-sixths of all matter in the universe, providing the gravitational force necessary to keep galaxies from spinning apart. While much remains unknown about this unseen material, including whether it exists, researchers have long considered black holes as potential candidates due to their extreme mass and difficulty in detection. The study specifically examined "stupendously large black holes" with masses greater than 100 billion times that of the sun. Objects in this category, particularly those weighing between one million billion and 10 million billion solar masses, would be heavier than whole galaxies. Currently, the largest known black hole weighs about 36 billion suns, and astronomers have not detected any stupendously large black holes despite observing numerous galaxies.

Christopher Gerlach, a theoretical physicist at the Mainz Institute for Theoretical Physics in Germany, noted that dark matter is typically conceptualized as a fine dust distributed throughout the cosmos. However, if dark matter were concentrated in a few gigantic objects like stupendously large black holes, the universe would appear grainy on very large scales. To test this hypothesis, the research team analyzed light from the early universe. Yann Gouttenoire, also of the Mainz Institute for Theoretical Physics, explained that for the first 380,000 years after the Big Bang, the cosmos was filled with hot plasma that trapped light. As the universe expanded and cooled, the plasma dissipated to form atoms, allowing light to travel freely. This light, known as the cosmic microwave background, serves as a snapshot of the infant universe covering the entire sky.

Antonio Iovino, a theoretical physicist at New York University, Abu Dhabi, in the United Arab Emirates, stated that the temperature of the cosmic microwave background varies by about one part in 100,000 from place to place. This pattern reveals how matter was distributed in the early universe. The analysis showed that the cosmic microwave background is not grainy in the manner that stupendously large black holes would have produced. Consequently, Nicholas Leister, a theoretical physicist at the Mainz Institute for Theoretical Physics, concluded that these massive black holes cannot constitute a significant portion of dark matter.

The researchers clarified that their findings do not rule out the existence of stupendously large black holes, only that they do not make up a major fraction of dark matter. They suggested that another potential candidate for dark matter is relatively tiny black holes the size of asteroids. The team is currently investigating whether such small black holes can be ruled out as a major constituent of the mysterious substance. The study detailing these findings is scheduled for publication on Oct. 26 in the journal Physical Review Letters.
summary: Researchers analyzed the cosmic microwave background to determine that black holes more massive than entire galaxies cannot constitute a significant portion of dark matter. The study indicates that such objects would have made the early universe appear grainy, a pattern not observed in the light from the dawn of the cosmos.

title: Griffin-1 lunar lander passes critical tests at NASA JPL
content:
Voyager Technologies’ Griffin-1 lunar lander has successfully completed a series of critical environmental tests at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California. The spacecraft underwent rigorous simulations designed to replicate the extreme conditions it will encounter during its journey to the moon, including intense temperatures, shaking, and acoustic noise from launch through landing. According to JPL, the lander passed these tests with flying colors. An image captured on August 31 shows the vehicle inside JPL’s 25-foot-wide space simulator, highlighting the facility’s role in preparing robotic explorers for mission-critical challenges.

Charles Whetsel, manager for the Exploration Systems Development Office at JPL, noted that the Environmental Test Laboratory has supported robotic missions since the Ranger program in the mid-1960s. He expressed pride in providing expertise and facilities to support the new phase of commercial lunar exploration. The Griffin-1 mission is scheduled to launch later this year as part of NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) initiative.

Upon reaching the moon, the robotic lander is expected to deliver over 1,100 pounds (455 kilograms) of cargo to a landing site near the lunar south pole. This payload includes science experiments and new technologies intended for surface testing. Among the cargo is Astrolab’s FLIP rover, which features a supercomputer designed to facilitate exploration of the lunar surface.

Beyond immediate scientific goals, the Griffin-1 mission aims to contribute to broader lunar development efforts. The data and experience gained from this robotic exploration will help prepare for the construction of a future crewed moon base. NASA plans to establish this base near the south pole within the next half-decade.
summary: Voyager Technologies' Griffin-1 lunar lander passed environmental tests at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory ahead of its scheduled launch later this year. The spacecraft will carry over 1,100 pounds of cargo, including Astrolab's FLIP rover, to the lunar south pole as part of NASA's CLPS initiative.

title: Taika Waititi’s Star Wars film joins unreleased Lucasfilm projects
content:
Taika Waititi has joined a long list of filmmakers who were expected to bring a new direction to the Star Wars franchise, only to find the studio appeared to get cold feet.  

The cost of producing a Star Wars film has risen sharply.  George Lucas’s 1977 original cost $11 million to make—about $60 million in today’s dollars—and has since earned $775 million at the global box office, including rereleases.  By contrast, the most recent entry in the saga, The Mandalorian and Grogu, reportedly cost $165 million and earned $346 million worldwide.  

Since 2019’s The Rise of Skywalker, only one Star Wars film—The Mandalorian and Grogu—has actually appeared in cinemas.  Yet Disney‑owned Lucasfilm has announced a small armada of other projects, often through press releases or at high‑profile celebrations, conferences and corporate jamborees, none of which has yet reached multiplexes.  The studio’s reluctance to produce new Star Wars movies has become a recurring theme in recent years.

title: Review: Crystal Lake suffers a bit from its obsession with Pam Voorhees
content:
Peacock’s new series Crystal Lake is positioned as a prequel to the original Friday the 13th film, though it initially diverges from the franchise’s typical horror tropes. The show aims to blend homage with uncharted narrative territory by providing a long-awaited backstory for Pamela Voorhees, the central antagonist of the 1980 movie. In the original film, Pam Voorhees shocked audiences by emerging abruptly during a killing spree and confronting the final girl with the chilling line, “Kill her, mommy,” delivered in the voice of her drowned son, Jason Voorhees.

Despite Jason Voorhees becoming the primary icon of the franchise, fans have remained fascinated by his mother, whose character was largely undefined. In the first film, Pam Voorhees was beheaded after only 13 minutes of screen time, and her spirit appeared sporadically in subsequent installments. The original actress, Betsy Palmer, who portrayed the character, refused to return for later films, a decision attributed to the lack of depth in the role. The new series, starring Linda Cardellini as Pam Voorhees, seeks to address this gap by exploring the character’s history.
summary: Review: Crystal Lake suffers a bit from its obsession with Pam Voorhees.
author: Ars Technica

title: Ukraine plans to fight without Starlink as Musk's political moves disrupt service
content:
Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite service has been a critical component of Ukraine’s defense against Russia’s full-scale invasion, providing high-speed internet and data streams for civilian and military use. The network has enabled Ukrainian forces to maintain vital communications and remotely control drones for air defense and offensive strikes. However, recent disruptions to service, attributed to Musk’s political actions, have made the system increasingly unreliable, prompting urgent discussions in Ukraine and Europe about alternatives.

According to an anonymous source from the Ukrainian defense company BlueBird Tech, Starlink remains the best available satellite coverage option due to its cost, availability, and ease of use, with virtually no competitors. The primary practical limitation identified is the need to position antennas correctly to receive satellite signals. As reliance on this single network becomes a security concern, Ukrainian and European officials are now facing the challenge of developing communication capabilities that do not depend on Starlink.
summary: Ukraine is facing urgent questions about how to proceed without Starlink due to recent service disruptions linked to Elon Musk's political inclinations. The satellite service has been critical for Ukrainian civilian communications and military operations, including drone guidance and air defense.
author: Ars Technica

title: US regulators warn Holtec International over safety concerns at Palisades reactor
content:
US regulators issued a warning to Holtec International, which is working to reopen the Palisades nuclear power plant in Michigan, following safety incidents where a contractor fell into a reactor cavity and fuel rods nearly tipped over during refuelling. The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission directed the company to address a “chilled work environment” that has left staff hesitant to report safety concerns for fear of retaliation.

Critics have raised concerns that financial and political pressures to revive the nuclear industry, part of Donald Trump’s efforts to meet booming AI-driven energy demand, are increasing the risk of accidents.
summary: US regulators warn Holtec International over safety concerns at Palisades reactor.
author: Ars Technica

title: EA closes BioWare, cancels Mass Effect: Universe, and cuts 400 jobs
content:
EA has announced the closure of BioWare, a game studio with a 30-year history known for role-playing games and choice-driven narratives. The decision results in the cancellation of its upcoming Mass Effect title and the loss of more than 400 jobs. The article’s author, Lucy James, a video games industry veteran and long-time fan, describes the closure as a significant loss for the RPG community.

The piece suggests that BioWare’s shutdown was driven by financial pressures on its parent company. EA is reportedly carrying $20 billion in debt following a leveraged buyout involving Jared Kushner and a Saudi wealth fund. While BioWare had a reputation for genre-defining titles like Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic and Dragon Age, the studio had not released a critical or commercial hit in over a decade.

The cancelled game, identified in a leaked trailer as Mass Effect: Universe, was originally announced in 2020. Although the project received some promotional attention, it remained years away from release at the time of the studio’s closure.
summary: EA announced the closure of BioWare, resulting in the cancellation of its upcoming Mass Effect game and the loss of more than 400 jobs. The decision follows a leveraged buyout that left the parent company with $20 billion in debt.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Young Americans choose Y2K cars over new SUVs
content:
Young Americans are increasingly opting for older, affordable vehicles over new SUVs, prioritizing cars they can purchase with cash and maintain independently. This trend defies the expectation that younger buyers will take on significant debt for new vehicles. Jack Price, a 30-year-old resident of Los Angeles, exemplifies this shift after joining the Marines in fall 2021. Unable to afford a new car, he spent a month searching dealer classifieds and Facebook Marketplace before his mother found a 2010 Volkswagen Jetta on an office listserv.

The vehicle, which had 60,000 miles on the odometer, was mechanically sound and equipped with a manual transmission, working air conditioning, a sunroof, and a Bluetooth radio. Price purchased the car for $6,000 in cash. He has since named the vehicle the "Pewter Pebble" and has driven it extensively, including cross-country trips and around military bases. Although he states he does not treat the car lovingly, he notes that while he receives criticism from older individuals, he does not face similar remarks from people his own age.
summary: Young Americans choose Y2K cars over new SUVs.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Experts Question Anthropic's Report on AI's Impact on Company Work
content:
Anthropic has released a new report outlining how artificial intelligence is reshaping work at the company and affecting labor demand. The report states that Anthropic is hiring fewer junior technical workers and that human attention has become the new “bottleneck” as the firm increasingly relies on its Claude AI agents.

Experts have expressed skepticism about Anthropic’s vision. The company’s CEO, Dario Amodei, previously warned that AI could eliminate half of entry‑level white‑collar jobs and that within six months it would write 90 % of code—predictions that did not materialize. The latest report reflects a shift in Anthropic’s strategy, emphasizing reduced junior hiring and greater dependence on AI agents.
summary: Experts Question Anthropic's Report on AI's Impact on Company Work.
author: Guardian Technology

title: EU-Canada associate membership needs institutional framework, Tobias Cremer says
content: European Parliament’s point man on Canada, Tobias Cremer, told Euronews that the planned “associate membership” should include an institutional framework formalising closer ties between the EU and Canada. He warned that the relationship needs more than warm words.
summary: EU-Canada associate membership needs institutional framework, Tobias Cremer says.

title: Typhoon Champi Causes Fatalities, Injuries, Flight Cancellations in Taiwan
content: Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan on Friday, sending towering waves crashing along the coastline. The storm left one person dead, 94 injured, and caused the cancellation of hundreds of flights.
summary: Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan, causing towering waves that crashed along the coast. The storm left one person dead, 94 injured, and hundreds of flights cancelled.

title: Shops in Lyon and Orléans barricaded ahead of National Rally congress and protests
content: Shopkeepers across France are erecting wooden boards to protect their premises amid concerns of potential unrest. The precautionary measures come as a National Rally congress is scheduled in Orléans, while protests are expected to approach Lyon. Businesses fear possible damage and disruption linked to the upcoming events.
summary: Shopkeepers in France are placing wooden boards to barricade their stores against possible unrest. The measures come as a National Rally congress takes place in Orléans and protests are approaching in Lyon, raising fears of damage and disruption.

title: Ukraine drones hit Yandex, Sber, VKontakte servers in five Russian regions
content: Ukraine’s drone attacks targeted Russian data infrastructure, striking three Yandex facilities, a Sber centre and a VKontakte server farm across five regions. The strikes caused persistent failures in payments, navigation and cloud services. Experts estimate that restoring the damaged infrastructure could take months or even years.
summary: Drones struck three Yandex facilities, a Sber centre, and a VKontakte server farm across five Russian regions, causing persistent failures in payments, navigation and cloud services. Experts say restoring the infrastructure could take months or years.

content: Storm Austen has struck France and the UK, producing huge waves, uprooted trees and damaged boats. In Brittany, gusts reached 160 km/h, while in southern England fallen branches blocked roads.
summary: Storm Austen produced huge waves, uprooted trees, and damaged boats in France and the UK. Gusts reached up to 160 km/h, battering Brittany and blocking roads in southern England with fallen branches.

content:
A multi‑storey building under construction collapsed in Nairobi, leaving a vast pile of rubble.  

Red Cross workers have arrived at the scene, where excavators are being used among the debris.

content:
A brutal targeted attack on an Australian female MP, who lost both her legs as a result, has reignited concerns over the rising levels of violence against women in public life.  

Cornell University is facing a no‑confidence vote over its handling of an alleged gang rape in 2024. Annette Young speaks to Annie E. Clark, a survivor of campus sexual assault, and Dr Sara Wilf of George Mason University about why institutions continue to struggle with sexual assault cases.

content: At least six people were killed and 28 wounded when unidentified assailants opened fire on a Greek Orthodox church during a funeral in the Karak directorate of central Jordan, authorities said on Friday. The attack targeted the congregation inside the church.

content: A suspect was arrested after a gunman opened fire from a vehicle in a Paris suburb on Friday, killing one person and wounding four others, including a 12‑year‑old girl. French authorities said the attack may have been racially motivated.

content:

summary: After more than three years of war, the number of Israeli soldiers suffering from post‑traumatic stress disorder following campaigns in Gaza and Lebanon has risen drastically. title: EU summit on Oct 15-16 ends without budget breakthrough, capitals deadlocked
content: A marathon EU summit on October 15-16 failed to produce a breakthrough on the European Union's next long-term budget. Although EU leaders put on a brave face at the end of the talks by saying that "the way forward is clearer", EU capitals appear deadlocked on what that path is. At stake is the EU's ability to finance its strategic priorities from 2028 to 2034. The main dividing line is between the so-called "frugal countries", who want deep cuts to the proposed budget, and the "friends of cohesion", who say that cuts are not the answer.
summary: The EU summit on October 15‑16 failed to reach a breakthrough on the Union’s next long‑term budget. Member states remain divided, with “frugal countries” pushing deep cuts and “friends of cohesion” opposing them, leaving the 2028‑2034 financing plan uncertain.

In a Talking Europe interview, Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna discussed the security situation in Estonia and the broader European Union.
summary: Estonia's counterintelligence service warned that sabotage operations orchestrated by Russian special services have entered a new dangerous phase in Europe, with targets no longer purely symbolic. content: Uganda has confirmed that it has no active Ebola cases. However, recent infections in Kenya and Nigeria have raised new concerns. Health officials are investigating whether Ebola patients from those countries crossed paths at Uganda’s main airport, as conflicting accounts have obscured the source of one infection.
summary: Uganda says it has no active Ebola cases. Health officials are investigating whether Ebola patients in Kenya and Nigeria crossed paths at Uganda's main airport amid conflicting accounts about the source of one infection.

content:
The United States has defunded one of the last universities that provided Afghan women the opportunity to pursue higher education following the Taliban takeover in 2021.  

DW interviewed a student who said she has lost hope of ever earning a degree.

content: New United Nations data released Thursday shows that, worldwide, mothers receive nearly eight times more paid leave than fathers. The disparity means women carry the majority of caregiving duties, which the report says imposes costs on families, children and economies.
summary: UN data released Thursday shows mothers worldwide receive nearly eight times more paid leave than fathers. The disparity leaves women to shoulder most of the care burden, costing families, children and economies.

content: A flash flood that devastated Nepal in August has been called a “defining moment” for both the country and the international community. The description comes from the head of the United Nations field agency that constructs roads, schools and clinics in crisis zones.

content: Prince William surprised viewers by appearing on The Graham Norton Show in a pre‑recorded episode that will air on BBC One on Friday. content: Exclusive: Key figure in campaign group accused of saying she would ‘never hire a black person’, and second figure discussed Sydney Sweeney’s ‘assets’ The Free Speech Union (FSU) is reeling from internal grievances involving allegations of racism, workplace discrimination and sexually inappropriate remarks by senior members of staff, the Guardian can reveal. title: Oil climbs above $115 a barrel as fears of US renewing Iran strikes rise
content:
Oil prices climbed above $115 a barrel on Friday, with Brent crude gaining about 1 % to reach its highest level since May and the highest point in more than five months. The rise occurred amid concerns that the United States could renew strikes on Iran, a fear highlighted in market commentary.

The price increase followed Tehran’s warning of possible retaliatory attacks on Gulf‑region refineries and data centres, prompting traders to brace for further escalation in the Middle East conflict. Energy markets responded to the heightened geopolitical risk with the noted surge in crude prices.
summary: Brent crude rose about 1% on Friday morning to above $115 a barrel, its highest level since May. The increase came as Tehran threatened retaliatory attacks on Gulf refineries and datacentres and markets feared the United States might renew strikes on Iran.

title: Netanyahu orders extensive West Bank operation after two soldiers killed
content:
Two Israeli soldiers and two Palestinians were killed in an exchange of fire near a checkpoint outside Hebron. The Israeli military said it had thwarted a “terror attack” carried out by two armed Palestinians on Friday.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered the army to prepare for a “very extensive” operation in the occupied West Bank. He said the military would go house to house and demolish homes in an operation on a scale unseen in the region for decades.

The incident comes amid heightened tensions as Israel approaches next week’s election.

title: Paris police fire teargas at New World Orchestra in Place de la République
content:
New World Orchestra musicians said they were shocked when French police used teargas against a peaceful gathering at Place de la République. Riot police encircled the square last week, firing teargas canisters to disperse demonstrators. Conductor Étienne Jarrier and his orchestra continued to play after most people had left, even as teargas was sprayed into the central Paris square.

Jarrier stopped the performance when he saw his musicians being hit directly. He told the Guardian that teargas canisters landed in double‑bass and music‑stand cases and ignited small fires that the musicians had to stamp out.
summary: Riot police encircled Place de la République in Paris and fired teargas canisters at a peaceful gathering. Conductor Étienne Jarrier said his New World Orchestra was directly hit, with teargas landing in double‑bass and music‑stand cases, so he ordered the musicians to stop.

title: Russia and Ukraine agree local ceasefire in Oleshky to aid civilians
content:
People in the Russian‑occupied city of Oleshky are facing severe shortages of food, water and electricity, with some reportedly surviving on weeds. The deepening humanitarian crisis has left thousands of civilians struggling to survive.  

The White House said on Friday that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a cease‑fire in Oleshky, halting all military operations from 29 October to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and preparations for civilian evacuation. Moscow and Kyiv have not commented on the development.
summary: The White House said Russia and Ukraine have agreed to halt all military operations in the Russian‑occupied city of Oleshky from 29 October to enable humanitarian aid deliveries and civilian evacuations. The city is experiencing severe shortages of food, water and electricity, with some residents reportedly surviving on weeds.

title: France to deploy about 70,000 police, including counter‑terrorism units, on Saturday
content:
France plans to deploy approximately 70,000 police officers nationwide on Saturday to prevent further civil unrest following severe street violence that occurred during cost-of-living protests last weekend. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez announced on Friday that the security deployment will include elite units typically reserved for counter-terrorism operations and hostage rescues.

The government’s intensified response follows a period described as the worst street violence in years. Nuñez also noted that social media platforms have seen calls for violence originating from “ultra-left” groups, prompting the inclusion of these specialized forces in the upcoming security measures.
summary: France will deploy about 70,000 police around the country on Saturday to prevent further civil unrest after recent street violence. title: Nigeria Ebola case source unclear; Swiss diplomat's wife likely infected in Uganda
content:
Health officials across Africa are working to determine how Nigeria’s first Ebola patient in more than a decade became infected, amid concerns that the outbreak could spread further after reaching a fourth African country. The case follows the virus’s detection in the Democratic Republic of Congo in mid‑May and its subsequent spread to Uganda, Kenya and now Nigeria.

Switzerland’s foreign ministry said the patient is the Ugandan‑born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja and that she had not travelled to the Democratic Republic of Congo. The ministry added that she is believed to have contracted Ebola while travelling with her husband in Uganda.
summary: Health officials across Africa are racing to determine how Nigeria’s first Ebola patient in more than a decade became infected. The Swiss foreign ministry said the patient, the Ugandan‑born wife of a Swiss diplomat in Abuja, likely contracted the virus while traveling in Uganda and had not travelled to the Democratic Republic of Congo.

content: Paris Saint‑Germain’s Ligue 1 fixture against Lyon at the Parc des Princes has been delayed by 24 hours. The postponement is linked to Paris’s preparations for another weekend of protests.

title: Rocket Lab launches three HawkEye 360 satellites into low Earth orbit
content: Rocket Lab launched a trio of private signals-intelligence satellites to orbit today (Oct. 23). The mission lifted off aboard an Electron rocket from Rocket Lab’s New Zealand launch site today at 3:11 a. M. EDT (0711 GMT; 8:11 p. M. Local time in New Zealand). The Electron carried three "Hawk" satellites for the Virginia-based company HawkEye 360, which explains the name Rocket Lab gave to the mission: "We're Not Hawking Around." If all goes according to plan, the three Hawks will be deployed into low Earth orbit (LEO), at an altitude of 323 miles (520 kilometers). Once up there and commissioned, the satellites will scan the globe for radio frequency (RF) emissions. "Operating in clusters of three, HawkEye 360's satellites collect signal data from across the RF spectrum for maritime tracking, GNSS jamming detection, radar monitoring, communications mapping and space defense," Rocket Lab wrote in a mission description. HawkEye 360 provides this data to the U. S. Government and its allies "to enable faster, better decision-making," according to the company. "Our space-based collection, proprietary signal processing and AI-powered analytics transform knowledge of the RF spectrum into a strategic advantage." The patch for Rocket Lab's "We're Not Hawking Around" mission. (Image credit: Rocket Lab) HawkEye 360's first satellites launched in 2018, and the company has now sent nearly 50 of them to LEO. The most recent Hawk launch before "We're Not Hawking Around" came just two days ago; three of the satellites went up on SpaceX 's Bandwagon-5 rideshare mission. "We're Not Hawking Around "was Rocket Lab's 98th launch to date and its 19th of 2026 so far. Sixteen of this year's flights have been performed by the two-stage, 59-foot-tall (18 meters) Electron. The other three have been conducted by HASTE, a suborbital variant of Electron that allows customers to test technologies in a hypersonic flight environment.
summary: Rocket Lab launched three HawkEye 360 satellites aboard an Electron rocket from New Zealand on Oct. 23, aiming to deploy them into low Earth orbit at 323 miles. The satellites will scan the globe for radio frequency emissions to support maritime tracking, GNSS jamming detection, radar monitoring, communications mapping and space defense.
author: Space.com

title: 11-year-old Bodhana Sivanandan nears youngest female IM chess record
content:
Bodhana Sivanandan, an 11-year-old chess talent from Harrow, England, is poised to break another world age record on Friday. She has already surpassed the 2400 rating threshold required to qualify for an open international master title, a milestone that allows her to join the ranks of the 10 youngest players in history to achieve that rating. This group includes notable competitors such as Roman Shogdzhiev, Nodirbek Abdusattorov, Faustino Oro, and Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus.

During this week’s European Club Cup, Sivanandan demonstrated strong performance against high-rated opponents. In round one, she narrowly missed a draw against former world title challenger GM Aleksandra Goryachkina. She later outplayed her IM opponent in round three, which raised her rating to 2399.4, just below the 2400 mark. In her subsequent game, she drew from a winning position against GM Nino Batsiashvili, who holds a rating of 2426.

Sivanandan’s achievements position her to become the youngest female international master in chess history, surpassing the existing world age record held by Judit Polgar. Her recent results in the European Club Cup have been instrumental in securing the final rating points necessary for this historic qualification.
summary: Bodhana Sivanandan, 11, requires a rating of 2400 to break Judit Polgar's world age record for the youngest female international master. She currently holds a rating of 2399.4 after competing in the European Club Cup against top grandmasters.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Is el clásico still the world’s biggest match? Three questions before Barcelona v Real Madrid
content:
The relevance of el clásico has diminished as the Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo rivalry faded, according to an article examining the fixture’s current standing. For nearly a decade, the match served as the defining narrative of soccer, extending beyond the pitch to influence Ballon d’Or voting and broader sports discourse during the peak of the two players’ competition. While the article notes that matches between Barcelona and Real Madrid have always mattered and will continue to do so, their cultural dominance has waned in recent years.

Looking ahead to 2026, the piece questions whether el clásico remains the sport’s biggest fixture, noting that it is now difficult to measure the match’s standing. The article poses the question of whether emerging talents Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappé can elevate the rivalry into a new era, challenging the previous narrative that defined the sport for a decade.
summary: The fixture’s relevance waned as the Messi-Ronaldo rivalry faded. Can Lamine Yamal and Mbappé lift it into a new era?

title: Chaotic state of football in Brazil epitomises a nation where greed has conquered glory | Jonathan Liew
content: The national game merely reflects the mood in a divided nation which is going to the polls with very little faith in the power of democracy Look, cards on the table: I don’t know for certain, and nor do you, whether Flávio Bolsonaro – the man widely tipped to become the next president of Brazil after Sunday night’s election – really did steal an island from Richarlison. There are lawyers involved, claims and counter-claims, and in any case, adjudicating land ownership disputes between right-wing strongmen and Tottenham reserve-team strikers lies very much beyond this column’s spectrum of expertise. It’s why, for example, this newspaper took no official position on the well-publicised battle between Rodrigo Duterte and Vincent Janssen over that Polynesian isthmus. According to Richarlison, a few years ago he purchased an island off the southern coast of Rio de Janeiro, and has the documentation to prove it. Richarlison says Bolsonaro tried to buy it from him, and when he refused a lawyer named Willer Tomaz simply turned up and annexed it. “These guys took the island without spending a penny, as far as I know,” Richarlison claimed in an Instagram video that has been viewed more than 31 million times. Tomaz has accused Richarlison of lying, arguing that he has a public deed registered at the notary’s office. Bolsonaro, for his part, has denied any connection with the island in question and described Richarlison’s intervention as “politically motivated”.
summary: Chaotic state of football in Brazil epitomises a nation where greed has conquered glory | Jonathan Liew.

title: Kimi Antonelli can become F1's youngest world champion at Austin
content: Mercedes youngster could become youngest title winner Max Verstappen says bumpy track makes drivers ‘suffer’ The Formula One world championship is within reach for Kimi Antonelli at the US Grand Prix in Austin this weekend. But while the young Italian approaches the race intending simply to have fun, there is disquiet among other drivers about the potential long-term health dangers posed by the state of the Texas circuit. The 20-year-old Antonelli will become Formula One’s youngest world champion if he claims the title at the Circuit of the Americas on Sunday, eclipsing Sebastian Vettel’s record from 2010, when the German driver was 23 and Antonelli was four.

title: Arbeloa cites improved transition after Hull win; Messi-Ronaldo era ends as Clásico looms
content:
Manchester United manager Ruben Amorim’s successor, Michael Carrick, faces potential dismissal as manager Steve Wilcox has expressed interest in appointing Eddie Howe if the Red Devils sack him. This personnel uncertainty coincides with a significant weekend in European football, highlighted by the upcoming La Liga clásico between Barcelona and Real Madrid at Camp Nou. The match is described as especially significant, with a Barcelona victory potentially extending their lead at the top of La Liga to nine points, while a Real Madrid win could serve as a catalyst for the remainder of their season.

In the Premier League, Fulham manager Álvaro Arbeloa addressed the team’s recent form ahead of their Saturday trip to Coventry. Arbeloa emphasized that the squad’s self-belief remained unchanged despite previous struggles against Manchester United and Ipswich. He noted that the recent win over Hull demonstrated improvements in transition and better ball control in the opponent’s half, which he identified as the most important aspect of that victory.

content:
The new smart adhesive patch sticks securely and releases gently without damaging skin.  
It addresses the sharp sting of removing a bandage, especially for people with fragile skin. Repeated attachment and removal can cause irritation, epidermal damage, and skin stripping in neonates, older adults, and critically ill patients.

title: No disease recurrences in 111 patients after short neoadjuvant immunotherapy (NICHE‑2)
content: A short course of neoadjuvant immunotherapy has shown sustained long‑term outcomes in patients with locally advanced mismatch repair–deficient (dMMR) colon cancer. In the NICHE‑2 study, 111 patients in the primary efficacy population were followed, and none experienced disease recurrence. All participants were alive at their most recent follow‑up. The results, published in The Lancet, add evidence to the durability of response to neoadjuvant immunotherapy in this patient group.
summary: In the NICHE‑2 study, 111 patients with locally advanced mismatch repair–deficient (dMMR) colon cancer received a short course of neoadjuvant immunotherapy and none experienced disease recurrence. All patients were alive at their most recent follow‑up, and the results were published in The Lancet.

title: Mindfulness and self-compassion can alleviate premenstrual symptoms
content: A recent study by psychologists at SWPS University and Jagiellonian University found that a kind attitude toward oneself and mindfulness practice can improve functioning in individuals who experience severe premenstrual symptoms. The research suggests that self‑compassion and mindful techniques may help alleviate the impact of these symptoms.
summary: A kind attitude toward oneself and practicing mindfulness can improve functioning in individuals who experience severe premenstrual symptoms, according to a study by psychologists from SWPS University and Jagiellonian University.

content: New research indicates that accelerated growth rates in Honeycrisp apples exacerbate the "bitter pit" disorder, increasing both its incidence and severity. content: Researchers have combined the ability to image individual atoms with the capacity to capture electron motion at ultrafast timescales. content: A new study reveals that glaciers terminating in lakes, oceans, or ice shelves represent just 3.2% of the world’s glaciers. Despite their small proportion, these glaciers lost 134 billion metric tons of ice annually between 2000 and 2019. This loss accounts for more than half of total global glacier ice loss during that period.

content:
Red crown rot, a fungal disease affecting soybean crops, is experiencing a surge across the Midwest after its initial report in Illinois in 2018. Boris Camiletti, a plant pathologist at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, is leading efforts to understand and combat the disease.

This initiative involves collaboration with the Crop Protection Network, the Illinois Soybean Association, the United Soybean Board, and researchers from surrounding states.
summary: Red crown rot, a fungal disease of soybean, is not new to the Midwest. First reported in Illinois in 2018, the disease is now surging across the state and the region.

content: A recent experiment published in Nature Communications demonstrated that AI agents assigned political positions and tasked with defending their views formed distinct political camps. Over repeated exchanges, the agents increasingly preferred interacting with those holding similar opinions. The study found that simply changing the agents' conversation partners did little to soften these hardened views.

content: A new report titled "InfoIA: Analysis of Information on Artificial Intelligence Published in Digital Media" reveals a significant gender disparity in Spanish news coverage of artificial intelligence. Conducted by the University Institute of Gender Studies at Universidad Carlos III de Madrid (UC3M), the study identifies a media "glass ceiling" in recent AI-related stories. title: Computational method reveals underestimated energy-loss mechanism in silicon carbide defects
content:
Researchers have addressed a longstanding challenge in understanding how tiny defects in materials such as diamond and silicon carbide behave under light exposure. By developing a new computational method, the team identified a significant energy-loss mechanism in silicon carbide that had previously been underestimated by scientists. This discovery resolves a mystery that has persisted for years within the field.

The findings provide new insights into the behavior of these defects and may enhance the design of quantum computers and sensors. The work highlights the importance of accurate computational models in predicting material properties for advanced quantum technologies.
summary: Researchers solved a long-standing challenge in understanding how tiny defects in materials like diamond and silicon carbide behave when exposed to light. Their new computational method revealed a surprisingly important energy-loss mechanism in silicon carbide that scientists had previously underestimated, which could improve the design of quantum computers and sensors.

content:
Scientists have uncovered a hidden messaging system in a tiny region deep within the brain.  
Unlike the previously assumed uniform chemical broadcast, this area sends targeted signals that help regulate learning, attention, and behavior, according to new research conducted in mice.
summary: A tiny region deep within the brain reveals a remarkably sophisticated communication system. Unlike previously thought, the region sends targeted messages that help control learning, attention, and behavior, according to new research in mice.

content: A seven-year study reveals that increased physical activity among people with Parkinson’s disease is associated with slower declines in memory, thinking, and movement abilities. Participants who exercised more than eight hours per week experienced almost no average cognitive decline, indicating that staying active may provide significant benefits as the disease progresses.
summary: A seven-year study found that people with Parkinson’s disease who were more physically active experienced slower declines in memory, thinking, and movement abilities. Those exercising more than eight hours per week showed almost no average cognitive decline, suggesting that staying active may offer important benefits as the disease progresses.

title: MIT engineers build light-controlled swimming robot using living muscle cells
content: MIT engineers have developed a paper-thin swimming robot powered by living muscle cells that react to light flashes. This design enables the device to swim and steer through water. The breakthrough may facilitate the creation of tiny, self-healing biological robots capable of exploring fragile environments that standard machines cannot safely navigate.
summary: MIT engineers have created a paper-thin swimming robot powered by living muscle cells that respond to flashes of light. This technology could enable the development of self-healing biological robots for exploring fragile environments.

content:
A newly FDA‑cleared PTSD treatment uses personalized brain mapping and magnetic stimulation to target abnormal brain activity in a clinical trial.

The trial reported a 52 % reduction in symptoms and a 68 % remission rate. Researchers say the technology could transform PTSD care and enable more precise treatments for other mental‑health conditions.

content: Researchers have found that dental implant infections can resist antibiotics because the implants themselves contribute to the problem. Bacteria corrode titanium implants, releasing microscopic particles that hijack immune cells, trigger destructive inflammation, and accelerate jawbone loss.

content: Switzerland’s glaciers are shrinking rapidly, with the country losing more than 5 % of its ice volume in 2026 alone. Several of the nation’s most famous glaciers recorded their worst melting on record, and several smaller glaciers have disappeared completely. Nearly 20 % of Switzerland’s glacier ice has vanished in just five years, driven by unusually snowless winters and extreme summer heat.
summary: Switzerland’s glaciers have lost more than 5% of their ice volume in 2026 alone. Nearly 20% of Switzerland’s glacier ice has disappeared in just five years, driven by unusually snowless winters and extreme summer heat.

title: Kikai Caldera's Magma Reservoir Refilled 7,300 Years After Major Eruption
content:
Scientists have discovered that a massive magma reservoir beneath Japan’s Kikai caldera is refilling, 7,300 years after one of the planet’s most powerful volcanic eruptions. Using underwater seismic surveys, researchers identified a vast store of magma that appears to have accumulated since the ancient catastrophe.  

The finding may shed light on how supervolcanoes such as Yellowstone and Toba rebuild their magma supplies, offering new insight into the long‑term dynamics of these powerful volcanic systems.
summary: Scientists used underwater seismic surveys to discover a massive magma reservoir beneath Japan’s Kikai caldera that is refilling 7,300 years after a major eruption. The finding may help explain how supervolcanoes such as Yellowstone and Toba rebuild their magma supplies.

title: Mass General Brigham AI model predicts cancer survival from selfies
content: Take a selfie to see how healthy you are: the idea is enticing and this new research is promising. But so many factors have been ignored The idea that a single selfie could predict how long someone with cancer may live sounds like an incredible breakthrough. AI is getting better at spotting patterns in medical data, but can it be used to reliably predict what will happen to an individual patient? I asked a clinical colleague what she thought about the recent headlines. She found it an interesting development given that doctors have long used facial appearance to assess patient health. For example, she noted that they may write “appears stated age” or “appears older than stated age” as a proxy for general health. Now, researchers from Mass General Brigham, a healthcare institution in Massachusetts, have taken this idea a step further. They have developed an AI model trained on more than 40 million facial images – called FAHR-Face – to assess biological age and predict survival in cancer patients. For biological age, they developed FAHR-FaceAge, which estimates age from certain facial features such as the forehead, the wrinkles between the nose and mouth and the temples. For cancer survival, they developed FAHR-FaceSurvival, trained using almost 35,000 photos of cancer patients. This model focused more closely on the area below the eyes and the bridge of the nose – regions of the face “ linked with dying ”. Dr Raymond Mak, one of the study’s authors, noted that these parts of the face are the same as those referenced by Hippocrates in 400BC as signs of muscle wasting and mortality risk: “the nose sharp, the eyes sunken, the temples fallen in”. Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh
summary: Researchers at Mass General Brigham trained an AI model called FAHR‑Face on more than 40 million facial images to estimate biological age and predict cancer survival. The FAHR‑FaceSurvival submodel uses nearly 35,000 photos of cancer patients, focusing on facial regions linked to mortality risk.

title: CoastSnap: Citizen Scientists Use Phone Cameras to Track Global Shoreline Changes
content:
Citizen scientists are now helping researchers monitor coastal changes using only an app and a camera phone. The program places a phone cradle and a sign at more than 200 spots worldwide, where participants can take a picture of the shoreline and send it to the project’s database.

Because shoreline positions shift with weather, tracking those changes over time is labor‑intensive. By encouraging everyday beachgoers to capture photos, the project turns a large workforce of camera‑phone users into a valuable resource for scientists.

The CoastSnap initiative began in Australia in 2017 and has since expanded to beaches around the globe. Each station includes a cradle to hold the phone while the photo is taken and a sign that explains where to send the snapshot.
summary: The CoastSnap project uses an app and a camera phone to capture shoreline photos at more than 200 spots worldwide, helping researchers monitor coastal changes. Started in Australia in 2017, the project now includes a cradle for phones and a sign that directs participants to send their snaps.
author: Guardian Science

title: Personalised mRNA vaccine intismeran cuts melanoma recurrence and death risk in trial
content:
A new clinical trial shows that a personalized mRNA‑based melanoma vaccine, intismeran, significantly reduces the risk of cancer recurrence or death within two years. The vaccine is custom‑made to target genetic mutations unique to each patient’s melanoma. Researchers described the results as a “foundational shift” in cancer treatment, highlighting the ability to harness the immune system in a more individualized manner.

Intismeran is the first individualized cancer vaccine to achieve positive outcomes in a phase III trial, marking the first time such a vaccine has demonstrated efficacy at this stage of testing.
summary: A personalised mRNA melanoma vaccine called intismeran, designed to target each patient’s unique tumor mutations, significantly reduced the risk of cancer recurrence or death within two years in a clinical trial. It is the first individualised cancer vaccine to show positive results in a phase III trial.
author: Guardian Science

title: Creator builds custom TV software with ML models after unwanted webOS update
content: A recent (unwanted) webOS update that got installed on TV prompted me to start going down the rabbit hole of writing new TV software. After a couple of weekends and massive help from 4 different models, finally managed to get v1 working. My daughter enjoys navigating TV through speech while I get to browse on the biggest screen at home. While all of the code was written by ML models, there were decisions I had to help with. In specific: using WebRTC to cut down latency, repurposing vendor logic for buffering voice samples and designing user experience. summary: The author wrote new TV software (v1) after an unwanted webOS update, with code generated by machine‑learning models and testing on four different TV models. title: iPhone Duo is not a small phone, unlike iPhone 13 Mini
content:
The recent review of the iPhone Duo clarifies that the device is not a small phone, despite its 5.4‑inch cover screen. The author notes that among the devices shown, only the iPhone 13 Mini on the left qualifies as truly small.

Readers who follow the iPhone 13 Mini expressed hope that the Duo might serve as a compact phone that expands into a tablet, but the review states that the Duo is “thick and heavy.” The author describes feeling its weight during everyday tasks such as reading email, scrolling Instagram, or placing it in a pocket, and characterizes it as a dense phone.

The reviewer also mentions personal use of an iPhone 13 Mini, which they keep despite its limited battery life that “barely lasts a full day.” The overall conclusion is that the iPhone Duo does not meet the expectations of Mini fans seeking a small, lightweight handset.
summary: The iPhone Duo is not a small phone despite its Mini‑ish 5.4‑inch cover screen. It is thick, heavy and feels dense when used, unlike the truly small iPhone 13 Mini.

title: Warhound startup to genetically modify dogs and add Anduril tech
content:
Warhound, a Texas‑based defense startup, has announced plans to genetically enhance military and police dogs and equip them with Anduril’s military technology. The company, founded by Anduril’s Palmer Luckey and Ben Lamm—co‑founder of Colossal Biosciences—has already secured $200 million in funding.  

Warhound will use Colossal Biosciences’ expertise in genetics, cloning, and animal biology to produce healthier dogs with traits suited to demanding missions. Anduril will then outfit the animals with its “advanced cybernetic Augments.” The Warhound website describes the initiative as “a new breed of dominance.”
summary: Warhound, a Texas‑based defense startup founded by Anduril founder Palmer Luckey and Colossal Biosciences co‑founder Ben Lamm, has raised $200 million. The company plans to genetically modify military and police dogs and outfit them with Anduril’s advanced cybernetic Augments.

title: Influential voices warn AI may trigger massive crises, citing Friedman's crisis theory
content:
An old policy concept is reappearing in public debate as a group of influential voices warns that artificial‑intelligence development may trigger crises of vast magnitude. The discussion centers on whether a guaranteed‑employment program could address potential mass AI‑related unemployment.

The conversation cites a passage from Milton Friedman’s preface to Capitalism and Freedom, in which he observed that “only a crisis – actual or perceived – produces real change” and that crises can bring once‑fringe ideas into the political mainstream. Friedman added that the role of intellectuals, think‑tanks and economists is to refine such ideas so that “good ones are ready when disaster strikes.”
summary: Influential voices predict that artificial intelligence could cause crises of vast magnitude. American economist Milton Friedman observed that crises bring fringe ideas into the mainstream and that intellectuals should refine ideas for disaster response.

title: MIT professor traces AI’s roots to early engineers injecting randomness
content:
Benjamin Lindquist, an assistant professor in MIT’s History Section and a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems, has explored the roots of modern artificial intelligence in a new paper published in Past and Present. In the article, Lindquist argues that early AI pioneers deliberately introduced randomness into deterministic algorithms to emulate the “messy” aspects of human thought. He traces the origins of what contemporary developers call AI hallucinations to these early experiments and warns that a balance between creativity and predictability will always be difficult to achieve.

Lindquist explains that the idea of injecting irrationality into machines was influenced by a broader mid‑century belief that chance plays a key role in discovery and artistic creation. He cites John Pierce, a prominent Bell Labs electrical engineer, who argued that mathematics could remove order from art and add unexpected bursts of irregularity. Early neural networks, built by psychologists, were intended to model the brain and reveal how it makes productive mistakes. These systems were not viewed as black boxes; researchers hoped they would provide insight into the messy processes of the mind. A competing view held that creative thinking was simply “normal” thinking performed more efficiently, and the debate centered on how to replicate human inventiveness in machine form.

According to Lindquist, the way early engineers approached AI differs from today’s focus on correctness. Early neural networks were prized for producing surprising, sometimes bizarre answers, whereas modern systems like ChatGPT or Claude are valued for giving reliable, expected responses. The shift has been driven in part by legal and monetary concerns that discourage unexpected or erroneous outputs.

Lindquist traces the historical trajectory of neural networks, noting that symbolic AI—an approach that represents knowledge in rules and propositions—dominated until the 1980s. The death of Frank Rosenblatt, a key figure in neural network research, in 1971 coincided with the rise of symbolic AI, though neural networks persisted in cognitive science. The availability of large data sets and increased computing power with the internet, and a breakthrough in 2012 when neural networks began outperforming statistical machine learning, shifted the field back toward data‑driven models.

Finally, Lindquist cautions that attempts to eliminate hallucinations may come at the cost of creativity. He stresses that the historical experience shows a trade‑off: making AI more predictable can unintentionally reduce its capacity for surprising, creative insights.
summary: Benjamin Lindquist, an assistant professor in MIT History Section, says early AI pioneers injected randomness into algorithms to mimic human creativity and produce hallucinations. He argues that tradeoffs between creativity and predictability will persist as AI systems are refined.

title: 2026 El Niño Mirrors 1997 Event, NASA Altimetry Shows Rising Sea Levels
content:
El Niño Then and Now

NASA Earth Observatory has released a pair of sea‑surface‑height maps that compare the 2026 El Niño event with the 1997‑98 and 2015‑16 outbreaks. The 2026 map, taken on October 12, shows higher‑than‑normal sea levels across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, a classic hallmark of El Niño. The pattern is almost identical to the October 13, 1997 map, which was captured during one of the strongest El Niño events recorded by satellite altimetry.

The altimetry data come from TOPEX/Poseidon for 1997, Jason‑2 for 2015, and the Sentinel‑6 Michael Freilich satellite for 2026. All three datasets were processed by scientists at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL). The maps illustrate sea‑level anomalies in shades of red (higher than average), white (normal), and blue (lower). Seasonal cycles and long‑term trends were removed so that the anomalies associated with El Niño and other short‑term natural phenomena stand out.

Josh Willis, JPL’s project scientist for sea‑level missions, notes that the 2026 event arrived more suddenly than the 1997‑98 event, but the two now appear similar in character. Both show a tilt of sea level—low in the west and high in the east—and high, warm water extending to South America. Willis suggests that the impacts could be comparable, citing the heavy rains that fell in California and the southern United States during the 1997‑98 event.

The 2015‑16 El Niño, while also strong, had a different pattern. The warm, high water along the equator did not reach the coast of South America to the same extent, producing rainfall that concentrated more over Central America and the southeastern United States. This difference is visible in the altimetry map for October 12, 2015, which shows a less pronounced elevation along the South American coast.

NOAA’s El Niño outlook released on October 8, 2026, called for an 83 percent chance of a strong‑to‑very strong El Niño through the first three months of 2027. Willis cautions that the chaotic nature of the atmosphere can alter the eventual impacts, noting that “just because this El Niño looks like 1997 doesn’t mean it will be exactly the same—it’s just our best guess at the moment.”
summary: 2026 El Niño Mirrors 1997 Event, NASA Altimetry Shows Rising Sea Levels.

title: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 review highlights North Korean invasion storyline
content: Activision; PC, PS5, Switch 2, Xbox From parkour over Manhattan rooftops and car chases in Paris to the climactic battle at a North Korean air base, the developers have thrown absolutely everything at the game And so we return perhaps one final time to Call of Duty’s Modern Warfare strand, with stories, “ripped from the newspaper headlines”, featuring shady terror organisations, nefarious rogue states and the brutally capable, monosyllabic war fighters who stand between us and Armageddon. Last year’s Black Ops 7 instalment was a sales disappointment for Activision, and that has no doubt put extra pressure on Infinity Ward, the studio leading Modern Warfare 4 development. Fortunately, this developer – like series heroes Price, Gaz and Ghost – seems to thrive on pressure. title: Leander Schaerlaeckens: Trump’s Fifa peace prize was a sham
content: The first awarding marked the apex of Gianni Infantino’s hubris. A new version could highlight the good in the world of soccer Sign up for our free newsletter here Poor Fifa peace prize. Unloved, unliked, mocked, tainted by association with its first winner. And now demoted, too, after Fifa’s president, Gianni Infantino, dumped the thing on the global governing body’s “social responsibility committee” to look after. To redeem it, rather than to ditch it, to spare Infantino the embarrassment of acknowledging that his fake prize was really just a fake prize all along. Here is where we should probably acknowledge that, as fake prizes go, and in the context of what it was intended to accomplish, the first awarding of the Fifa peace prize was an unqualified success. It achieved exactly what it was meant to, made by Infantino to flatter Donald Trump, the man he needed to keep on his side to safeguard the riches to be extracted from the North American market in order to consolidate his power base within Fifa. Trump, the gullible buffoon, was pleased as punch – handed a big, golden bauble and a medal he placed around his own neck – and briefly forgot about the Nobel peace prize he desperately covets. Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: US Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts, which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.
summary: Author Leander Schaerlaeckens argues that the first Fifa peace prize awarded to Donald Trump was a fabricated creation by Gianni Infantino designed to flatter the former president. In 2023, Lisa Watson-Morgan, the then-director of NASA's Human Landing System, told Ars that while the agency had a general idea of the requirements, she was reluctant to state the exact number. title: Switch 2 partially jailbroken via SmileBasic 4 integer overflow
content:
Security researcher Sammy Hajhamid has demonstrated a software-only, tethered jailbreak for the Nintendo Switch 2, achieving "userland" access. According to Hajhamid, this vulnerability enables users to run homebrew software, reverse engineer and modify games, back up save files, and access most of the console’s peripherals through MMIO. The exploit relies on the original Switch version of SmileBasic 4, a programming environment and interpreter for Nintendo hardware.

The hack requires a macOS or Linux PC on the same network to run a specific node that facilitates privileged system access. Hajhamid developed a custom harness to send USB commands to the system and view results via HDMI, using a Bluetooth light switch to power cycle the device. He utilized OpenAI's Codex to analyze SmileBasic’s language interpreter over a two-week period.

The process identified a 32-bit integer overflow that occurs when removing items from an array in SmileBasic. This error provides access to an array pointer, which grants read and write access to portions of the system memory.
summary: Security researcher Sammy Hajhamid demonstrated a tethered software-only jailbreak for the Switch 2 using an integer overflow in SmileBasic 4. This exploit grants userland access to run homebrew, reverse engineer games, and back up save files.

The discussion focused on preventing potential violence at upcoming demonstrations, including a Saturday protest called by the “Yellow vests” movement. The report was provided by FRANCE 24’s Luke Shrago.
summary: French PM Sebastien Lecornu held a meeting with leaders of political parties after unrest this weekend across the country. The aim was to prevent potential violence during the next protests, including on Saturday as the "Yellow vests" movement called for a new mobilisation.
author: France 24

title: Ten Years After Cameroon Train Disaster, Victims Await Justice
content: Ten years after Cameroon’s worst railway disaster, victims are still awaiting justice. A Cameroon National Railway Intercity train derailed on the Yaounde‑Douala line, killing 79 people and injuring hundreds.
summary: A Cameroon National Railway Intercity train derailed between Yaounde and Douala, killing 79 people and injuring hundreds. Ten years later, victims are still awaiting justice.
author: France 24

title: Italian truckers block roads in protest over soaring diesel prices
content: Italian truck drivers have blocked refineries and key roads in protest of soaring diesel prices. The government has warned that such blockades could result in criminal penalties, and authorities are working to clear the demonstrations. The report was provided by FRANCE 24 correspondent Seema Gupta in Rome.
summary: Italian truck drivers have blocked refineries and key roads to protest soaring diesel prices. Italy’s government warns that truckers blocking roads could face criminal penalties as authorities move to clear demonstrations.
